[h1]🟩Pros[/h1]
+Polished VR Experience
+Proper Half-Life game
+Comfortable to play
+Insane level of detail
+Excellent Storytelling
+Immersive Gameplay

[h1]🟥Cons[/h1]
-Lack of melee combat

[h1]🎮Half-Life: Alyx[/h1] An immersive single-player narrative experience that looks, feels, and plays exactly like what you would expect from a Half-Life game. From the gunfights, interactable objects, physics engine, brilliant storytelling, memorable characters, to the immersive environments/levels. This game has got it. 

[h1]📜Level of detail[/h1] 
We’re back to City 17. A very familiar place for Half-Life fans, seeing it in VR with Valve’s modern engine and masterful graphics is jaw-dropping. The city is more detailed than ever; more stuff to pick up, and more objects to interact around. Despite that, it still feels a lot like the city we’ve played in more than a decade ago.

Unlike most VR games, Half-Life: Alyx does not try hard to make itself too realistic when it comes to VR interactions with the environment, especially with the inventory system. Having said that, there is no HUD. Everything is displayed on Alyx’s gloves and weapons instead.

You don’t have to get every weapon/item from all around your body, instead they’ll mostly come from a few conveniently well-made simple hand gestures and additional slots for each of your wrists. Ammunitions for reloading that you get from over your shoulder are automatically selected based on the weapon you’re holding. Valve really found the right balance of realism and mechanics here and I love their take on it. Everything feels natural.

As with your interactions with the environment, it is insanely detailed. It’s like another level of detail comparable from the jump in detail from 3rd person to 1st person. Now this is 1st person going to VR. Everything seems kind of personal and big. NPC’s are big and detailed, just as big or bigger than me. Objects seem like real objects. Enemies feel really threatening.

Almost everything can be picked up. Jars, bottles, glasses, crates, boxes, can be broken. TVs thrown around. Cabinets, drawers, opened. You might even find yourself an ammo or two inside these containers. They also solve the VR item pickup conundrum by the use of Alyx’s gravity hands. It’s no gravity gun from HL2; Much, much weaker, only enough for you to fling almost any small object for you to catch it. No need to walk over an item and crouch down to pick it up.

[h1]⚔️Combat[/h1]
Continuing the trend of balancing realism vs mechanics, the combat is very well done. You can really feel the weight of the guns as well as their power when shooting. Aiming is accurate and the rumble feedback to my controllers are just right. The reload system they’ve implemented is smooth and reliable. Consistent and repeatable. Fuck ups are more on you than on the game’s mechanic. 

You can also upgrade your guns through the use of ‘resins’ which are scattered and collected throughout the game. Upgrades like reflex sight (which I hated), and extended magazines are available. I wished they included an option to remove the sights though once I upgraded it as personally I was more comfortable using the iron sight.

The enemies, ranging from the mindless zombies, headcrabs, to the combine forces are all back and have been improved upon. Zombies and headcrabs are more unpredictable this time, making them harder to hit. Combine forces can now survive more gunshots, some can deploy shields, and can even deploy Manhacks of their own.

With it’s reputable physics engine and VR implementation, Valve missed a huge opportunity with the non-existent melee combat. Nothing can be used for melee: Pipes, bars, concrete blocks, barrels, even guns cannot be used for melee. Melee combat is basically null in this game.

You cannot even take advantage of the physics engine to kill off people like throwing stuff at or dropping things on them. For a game that has the crowbar as a series staple, the gravity gun as another, this game has none of any of that.

[h1]📖Story[/h1]
The story is well written and engaging. It fleshes out Eli and Alyx’s stories even more. It gives you an idea of what their order of business was like before Gordon Freeman came along. Playing Alyx is somewhat a nice change of pace from playing Gordon Freeman again, it retracts that subconscious idea that your character is a total badass and can single-handedly destroy the enemy. A feeling that we have when playing badass FPS characters like Gordon, Masterchief, Doom Guy, etc. It makes for a game that has a character that seem normal, average, “not the chosen one”, and haven’t proven herself yet. That Half-Life vibe is still there though, especially the humor, bleakness, and mysterious nature. 

And it’s not just a side-story or a spin-off; other games are referenced in a much more direct and substantial way. To simply explain without spoilers, you definitely need to have played this or at least watched online before you play any future Half-Life games set after Episode 2.

[h1]🗺️Level Design/Pacing[/h1]
Personally I used the full locomotion option as I am playing wirelessly. The FPS-like free movement is handled perfectly. I’ve encountered no dizziness whatsoever. As opposed to other VR games where I’m dizzy 15 minutes in, this one I can play for hours. I think it has something to do with the movement speed which is just perfect for me although some may say it’s a bit slow. 

The level design is perfect for a VR game. Maps are big and spacious, there’s plenty of room to move around and explore while still preserving that linear map design. You will most certainly find yourself to the next area and you won’t get lost all the time trying to find the next corridor or door to open. 

Unfortunately for a VR game, loading screens are still a thing, as the classic Half-Life in-between level loading screens are back. Although they are much more bearable now with a holographic city-map view of your progression ala-Metro 2033 instead of just dull frozen moments with a “Loading” text at the center.

There are different types of puzzles in the game. One example are the level puzzles where you need to use physics or interactables; maybe you need to stack some crates, activate some levers, press some buttons, or provide power to some contraption. The transition from pressing a button to VR made all the difference. There are also the various mini-game hacking puzzles that are pretty entertaining. Puzzles are not too hard but will still give you a challenge. Some are straightforward, some might require a bit of critical thinking to solve. They get harder and harder as you progress through.

And of course it isn’t Half-Life without a bit of horror and creepiness. Especially in one part, which is my favorite to say the least. I would say this is where I got the most immersion out of HL: Alyx and one of the strongest points. Truly one of the most horror experiences I had with a video game. This one part terrified me to the point that I was jumping around while playing! And they weren’t using jump scares or any cheap tactic. You’ll definitely know it when you see it.

[h1]🖥️Technical Performance[/h1]
The game runs smoothly even with the resolution set to 120% on my rig: i7-8700k, 32GB RAM, and GTX 1080. No crashes, game-breaking bugs, or major glitches I've encountered. Using an Oculus Quest with ALVR, I was able to play wirelessly and experience free stick movement scheme to its fullest.

[h1]⚖️Conclusion[/h1]
While Half-Life: Alyx does not directly continue the series (as obvious in the title), It signifies Valve’s return to form when it comes to making singleplayer games, and they certainly deliver. If this is just Valve’s toes in the water into the Half-Life making business again, then I’m excited for what’s to come.

Valve doesn't just use new technology because it exists, but because they know how to make the best use of it, and they have just proven it again. Half Life games were always about innovation, which is why VR was the next logical step for the franchise.

The interactions with the motions controls and especially the gloves are well executed and a lot of fun. It results in a dynamic and diversified gameplay.
The visuals and sounds with Source 2 are really impressive. Everytime I walk into an outside environment it's just a "wow" moment where I will just stand around and look at the beautifully designed levels. Nevertheless it's well optimized, I can run the game on the highest preset while my hardware is not the latest any more. 

I love the fact that Valve stays true to themselves. While VR obviously changes a lot in terms of controls and interaction, the game still feels like a real Half-Life game. This goes from well known characters like Alyx and Eli Vance, over the beautiful environments of city 17, to the familiar sounds from the healing stations, combine chatter and more. 

However this Half-Life is very different to it's predecessors in terms of gameplay (apart from the obvious changes for VR motion controls/ interactions): You cannot sprint or free jump any more (just by teleport), which makes the game much slower. Valve did this for a "comfortable" gameplay for everyone. Still this is a thing they should have handled differently. 
Also I don't get why there is no melee combat at all, I mean you cannot even damage enemys by throwing heavy objects at them.

Anyway HL Alyx is easily the best VR game yet, just how people expected. I can only recommend to play it yourself. Watching videos of other people playing can not even closely give you the same level of immersion, intensity and fun you experience using a VR headset.
So if you still don't own one, there's never been a better time to get into VR!


EDIT: Completed the game after almost 11 hours of total playtime which I did in just two play sessions.
The ending blew me away and also made me shed some tears... Half-Life fans will definetly understand. What an outstanding game. I could not be more grateful to Valve for getting back at Half-Life. Hopefully this is just the beginning!

This should be an indication of how much I enjoyed playing it.

It took me four years to justify purchasing a virtual reality headset [i]just[/i] to play Half-Life: Alyx, and probably due to procrastination this time never came. Luckily, over the festive period I received a Quest 3, and with my immediate delight I knew exactly what game I needed to try first.

I’ve been able to play through the game twice now, the latter whilst holding on to the iconic Gnome Chompski (my final achievement [i]Gnome Vault of My Own[/i]). 

As an immersive experience, I’m absolutely blown away by the numerous moments of wonder, excitement, goosebumps & jump scares scattered throughout the campaign. The world feels so alive. I’ve had literal moments where I’ve stood and stared, with an open mouth, in complete disbelief. A bit about VR in general:
The VR world currently consists mostly of experiences.
There are experiences of exploring real or imaginary worlds... 
Working out... 
Playing physical games... 
Experiencing interactive stories unfold around you... 
Shooting at things and blowing things up...
Riding roller coasters...
Shooting bows and slashing people with swords...
etc. etc.

The basic idea is you experience some kind of activity, but it's in VR, so you feel as if you're physically in that experience and/or physically interacting with objects around you.
The experiences can be mediocre and can be amazing and fun.
But they always remain just that - experiences.
None of them amounts to an actual game - with story, plot, game world, game mechanics, progression, etc. etc.
There are some games that could be called casual/mobile/indie games.
But no games that would be considered an AAA game on PC or even on a console.

And even those that come close (the Walking Dead, Call of Duty, Fallout VR, etc.) - feel more like a PC/console port for VR, rather than a native VR game.
And unfortunately do many things wrong, making the experience ultimately unenjoyable at some point.
While HL:A is both an AAA game, and a VR game built specifically with VR in mind.


Specifically about HL:A :
This is the first game I've encountered in VR, which at the same time:
1. Has AAA-game polish, quality and size
2. Has been built with VR in mind, doing every possible thing in VR exactly right
3. Gives amazing value even after you finish the game

Let's delve into each for a second:
Polish:
The game is polished like almost no other VR game. 
I've encountered no crashes, games-breaking bugs, or even getting stuck in badly designed spots forcing you to reload your game.
The levels are not huge, but allow you to roam free, almost making it feel like an open world game.
Wherever you go, everything is polished and thought out.

Graphics:
Graphics quality is amazing!
The only thing limiting me is my GPU and VR helmet, as I upgrade over time, I'm sure the game look even better.

Size:
The scope of the game is like an actual AAA game, somewhere between 15 - 20 play hours.
Far from the 1-2 hour length of the usual VR "experience".

Plot/Story/Dialogs:
Unlike most VR FPS games/experiences, where you take a gun and just start shooting.
HL:A is more of a full-fledged game.
You have an engaging plot.
An interesting story to discover.
Dialogs you enjoy listening to.
All the benchmarks of a good AAA game.

VR physics:
The physics in the game feels very life-like, and very much as it should.
The problem with walking around and bending over (or squatting) to pick every item you find was elegantly solved by the "gravity gloves" which allow you to pull things towards you, without you actually bending over (or jumping) to pick them up.
A very elegant solution for a VR game.

VR world:
The world around looks very real, and very alive.
So much so, that even exploring scenes or levels from the game, is offered as a VR experience outside the game.
Just walking around in the HL:A level/environment, is comparable to playing a VR game/experience.

VR comfort level:
One of the main issues with most VR games, is their poor comfort level.
The bad games disorient you completely.
And even some of the better ones (especially first person shooters), can make you physically nauseous / queasy.
This is due to the "locomotion" effect.
When you move/glide inside a game, your eyes are sending signals that you're moving, while your body is sending signals you're standing still.
This causes a cognitive dissonance in your brain, which causes nausea.
Some people are more susceptible to this, while others are less. And it even changes as you age.
So making a comfortable VR experience, can be a difference between a great game you enjoy... and a great game you can't stand for more than 10 minutes at a time.
This has been a known issue in the VR world from the very beginning, and games have discovered many ways around it:
Snap turns instead of gradual turns, skipping climbing sequences, no tilting/staggering while moving around, jumping/teleporting around instead of walking/sliding, etc.
HL:A simply uses all of them. It simply allows you to use any comfort settings available in any other game. Surprisingly few games in the VR world do.
And the bottom line is: This is the only FPS game in VR I'm able to play indefinitely without getting nauseous.
My limitation now is the battery life of my headset, instead of the rising need to throw up.
This alone makes it one of the best VR games ever.

Performance:
I'm personally playing the game on Oculus Quest 2, which has some advantages and disadvantages:
Its resolution is one of the best available in 2021, even though the refresh rate can be better.
The other great thing is that it's completely wireless, and works great with a Wifi connection.
So while my gaming rig sits in a small/cramped room, I'm actually playing my games in my spacious living room / bedroom, with plenty of room to walk around.

The flip side, is that instead of only needing to render the images on screen, my PC needs to stream the images to the headset.
And while my GPU was considered high-end at the time (AMD Vega 64), it's quite a few years old by now, can now be compared to a mid-range graphics card. So for running HL:A and streaming it to my headset, I need to close every possible application running on my PC, and it still barely manages to handle the load.
So I would definitely recommend a more beefy graphics card when streaming HL:A to Oculus Quest 2.

Oh, and I almost forgot:
The fact that as usual Valve made the game very moldable, gives amazing value even after you finish the game.
A mere year after the game was released, there already exists a mod that allows you to play the entire Bioshock 1 in VR (as a mod of HL:A).
I'll let that sink in for a second:
You get the ability to play Bioshock. An amazing game in its own right. Completely immersed in VR. Completely for free.
That's simply mind-boggling...


In conclusion:
I would say HL:A is VR's killer app.
This is a must-have to any VR enthusiast, and will be the benchmark to which every new game is compared.

It’s difficult to talk about Half-Life: Alyx.

Hell, it’s difficult to talk about Half-Life period.

As a fan since the very beginning, I’ve been through the dizzying highs and the seemingly interminable lows. Episode Two remains the single greatest video game experience of my entire life, but the years after its release (the “dark interval” I morbidly call) were excruciating to endure. My perception of the series is now inextricably conflated with vivid memories of frequent frustration at VALVe’s vagaries along with intermittent bouts of sweeping hope followed swiftly by crushing disappointment. Key members of the original Half-Life team retired in quick succession during the 2010s, capped off by the departure of writer Marc Laidlaw in 2016. This was the death knell, signalling the end of the series as I knew it.

I subsequently settled into a state of perpetual dissatisfaction and melancholy. Laidlaw offered ‘epistle 3’ as tiny consolation, but there was no real closure. No catharsis. Just constant yearning for a conclusion that I was forced to accept would never come.

Then, like a quantum fluctuation, Half-Life: Alyx was announced out of nowhere.

I experienced an avalanche of conflicting thoughts and feelings competing for dominance – shock, excitement, disbelief, disappointment, apprehension and more. Like a monkey’s paw, my wish had been granted but not without a few caveats. This was a prequel, not a sequel. This was a full-fledged game, but VR-exclusive. This was made by VALVe, except without Laidlaw and various other OG developers.

This was new Half-Life, but not the Half-Life I had hoped for.

Despite my misgivings, I couldn’t miss out on such a momentous event. I upgraded my PC and purchased a Samsung Odyssey+ – an unprecedented investment for just one game, but which only Half-Life could entice me to make. Alyx launched almost as soon as COVID lockdowns began worldwide and I completed it within four days.

The first few hours of Alyx were astonishing. I was expecting to be impressed based on the trailers I watched but, having never played VR before, I was still unprepared for the jaw-dropping detail, scale and immersion. It was incredibly emotional returning to a world I had been obsessed with as a teenager – one I had thought abandoned just a few months earlier – let alone through VR. I can find no words with which to adequately describe how affecting it was to fade in on that balcony and see that familiar vista – the monolithic and parasitic Citadel towering above the meagre housing blocks of City 17 and its hapless citizens. 12 very long years fell away the instant I heard the distinctive ambiance of Combine dropships, scanners and hunter choppers swarming the surrounding sky as the clinical and artificial voice of the omnipresent Combine Overwatch pierced the air.

I was also unprepared for the grueling physical demands of playing VR and it was intensely visceral at regular intervals. One moment that stands out is approaching a hanging corpse at the end of a dark canal and reaching for its flashlight, knowing something monstrous will emerge when I take it. The dread is palpable and minutes pass before I work up the nerve to continue. As soon as I grab the flashlight, I whirl around and see the unmistakable silhouette of poison headcrabs scuttling towards me, barely visible in the dark. Panic stricken, I flail around the area, waving the flashlight wildly and emptying my shotgun recklessly, barely dodging their leaps as they approach me. Not since the days of the original Half-Life has the lowly headcrab provoked such fearful, primal and instinctual reactions in me.

Less frightening but no less thrilling was my first proper engagement with Combine soldiers. I exit a subway tunnel, the sound of gunfire close by. My way forward is momentarily blocked by a stationery Razor Train beyond which Combine chatter signal the presence of two grunts. The train starts to accelerate, the gaps between each carriage briefly revealing their positions. The first notes of 'Anti-Citizen' kick off and an unexpected rush of adrenaline courses through me as the firefight begins. Old memories of holding off waves of Antlions alongside Vortigaunts in a mine and surviving an ambush at an abandoned inn come flooding back as I duck behind concrete and dispatch them.

Glorious.

These encounters would have been child’s play with a mouse and keyboard. In VR, fending off headcrabs, avoiding barnacles and engaging in firefights with just a handful of Combine soldiers was far more difficult and taxing than it had ever been before. Everything was much slower, more deliberate, more threatening. More realistic. Fitting, really, given the change in protagonist. Alyx has always been so much more human and more vulnerable than Freeman ever was. Hell, the immense detail in the environment alone was often exhausting to look at and process. I spent obscene amounts of time reading newspapers, examining flora, poking at zombie corpses and inspecting objects. The headset itself was also challenging to wear for extended periods of time and each session rarely lasted longer than an hour and a half, by which time my head was pounding severely and I had no choice but to take a break.

Suffice to say, I really enjoyed Alyx.

But I didn’t quite love it.

The gameplay and overall presentation was exemplary, but the narrative was thin even by Half-Life standards. Substantive story beats were few and far between, filled in by far too many quippy interactions between Alyx and Russel. The latter overstayed his welcome during the second half of the game, at which point Eli should have had a more prominent presence. I was particularly troubled by the ending, which effectively erased the horror and anguish of Episode Two’s cliffhanger while blowing the proverbial lid open on what the G-Man is capable of doing with little regard for the messy implications therein. It seemed to me to be a transparently desperate and potentially ill-fated attempt to wriggle out of a deep crevice in which VALVe had become hopelessly stuck for over a decade and to reorient the future of the series following the departure of some of its original auteurs, leaving me with decidedly mixed feelings.

Four years passed in the veritable blink of an eye and I found myself compelled to play Alyx again a few weeks after the 25th anniversary of the series. My first – and only – playthrough had come with a lot of baggage. Hype and expectations rarely invite a balanced perspective and mine was certainly clouded by both. In addition, I’d rushed the second half of the game to get to the ending and avoid spoilers, failing to absorb and appreciate some of the details and moments along the way. This time, I intended to take my time without any of the noise, novelty or cynicism getting in the way. I wanted to see the game for what it really is.

And it’s truly a masterpiece.

Alyx reaffirms that VALVe is simply without equal as a developer. It’s several orders of magnitude above every other VR title to date, a superlative game period and a worthy addition to this highly esteemed series, once again pushing the frontier of gaming in the way only Half-Life – only VALVe – has ever done. The environments are stunning, the puzzles satisfyingly tactile, the combat exhilarating and the performances top-tier. I especially like how Alyx imitates the structure of Half-Life 2, using each chapter to introduce and focus on a new gameplay idea or mechanic. It’s still not narratively substantive and some of my misgivings about the ending remain, but it succeeds where it matters and leaves room to do a lot more.

Indeed, perhaps the best thing about Alyx is that it ends with the promise of more Half-Life to come one day. For a few precious moments, inhabiting Gordon Freeman again, a radiant light wiped away the darkness of that devastating cliffhanger, offering a brief glimpse beyond its event horizon.

Half-Life has a future once more.

Just completed the long-awaited playthrough of [b]Half-Life: Alyx[/b], and I'm sharing some fresh impressions.

[b]Alyx[/b] serves as a bridge between the games of what we might call the past (from a 2020 perspective) and the future. It shows us what games can and will be. That very first scene is breathtaking—you’re standing on a rooftop in [i]City 17[/i], and you’re overwhelmed. You lose yourself for a good half hour, sketching on the wall with markers. And when you’re hiding from [i]Jeff[/i], literally holding your hand over your mouth (both in the game and in real life), your heart pounds. You’re terrified to even turn your head, let alone make a sound. When you finally get to the “[i]Vault[/i],” you’re having the time of your life, using your hands as if they’re a gravity gun.

Here’s what I’ll remember forever:

[list]
 [*]The [i]Strider[/i] battle. The power of VR and controllers hits its peak here. Reload, aim, fire; reload, aim, fire. Amazing.
 [*]The space and time distortions in the final chapter are spectacular. I wanted to stretch that moment, jump from the ceiling to the walls, manipulating objects like magnets.
 [*][i]Jeff[/i]. Good ol' Jeff. You just have to get used to him, as Alyx rightly notes.
 [*] The music and visuals are top-notch. I loved the deep crimson hues, the palette of greens and blacks that appear when you’re disconnecting the floating “[i]Vault[/i]” from its gravitational tethers.
[/list]

All this alone is enough to give the game an 8.5 out of 10.

However, there are some downsides, mostly related to the game design.
[list]
 [*]The puzzles. Linking up the electricity lines behind walls becomes annoying and tedious. You start sighing heavily, looking for yet another junction to connect the wires. At this point, [b]Alyx[/b] stops being a game and starts feeling like a monotonous, dull task. The chapter with the electric dog—where you need to extract energy to advance—is a slog. It’s one of those sections you never want to replay. I watched a playthrough on YouTube where someone installed a mod that auto-solves the puzzles. I get it.
 [*]Lack of melee weapons. The game turns into an endless episode of [i]Ravenholm[/i] with constant ammo rationing. Except in [i]Ravenholm[/i], you had sawblades and a gravity gun.
 [*]The environments. The initial excitement fades into a feeling of “closeness.” There are almost no open spaces, just occasional courtyards. Soon enough, the sense of grandeur gives way to a local, confined vibe.
[/list]

Perhaps these downsides are simply design choices to extend the game’s length. But the game doesn’t need artificial padding—you’d return to it anyway.

This game has been a long time coming (thanks to VR), and the experience is truly indescribable. Once again, Valve has set an incredibly high bar for game creation. [b]Alyx[/b] stands as a full-fledged chapter in the series, both a prequel and a continuation. The impact on culture and [i]Half-Life fans[/i] is immeasurable.

The verdict: play it. Absolutely play it.

VR is an amazing medium. It often has to live within the confines of a smaller scope due to the computing overheads to run true stereoscopic 3D for VR being so much higher than your standard game.

As an example, The Oculus Quest 2 (which is your entry-level VR headset for gaming) runs at a resolution of 1832x1980 per eye - you need higher resolutions on what amounts to such tiny displays because they're right up against your eyes, and you're looking at them through a magnifying lens. Standard HD is 1920x1080 so outputs around 2M pixels per frame. The Quest 2 is outputting 3.6M pixels per frame [i]per eye.[/i].

So that means the output is already closer to 4K - but this isn't a case of "Well my GPU can run 4k60 on better looking games no problem", you have to remember that each eye on your VR headset is being shown [i]different images[/i], which takes even more GPU power to do.

That's why VR games always seem graphically simple in comparison to flatscreen games. Look at things like Until You Fall, Superhot VR and  Into The Radius - all awesome games, but there are either aesthetic decisions to make the graphics look more stylised or cartoony, or the graphics are toned down to look more like a game which could have come out as a flatscreen game in the mid 2000's. You often find this is one of the arguments against VR (usually from the people who don't have a VR headset) - that too many compromises have to be made. However most people who have experienced VR understand that VR isn't just a subsection of console or PC gaming: it's an entire medium on its own, and most developers are in that awkward stage of a mediums early-life where they're still experimenting to find out what works best: and most people understand that the the draw of VR tech is the immersion that it offers - not amazing graphics or deep, complex gameplay. This is why games like Arizona Sunshine and Pavlov VR still consistently sell well in the VR community: 2 games that, by all accounts, would be derided and panned as being stuck in the early 2000's, still loved because everything that people would consider is an important facet of a modern game becomes secondary to the level of immersion and interaction that VR can afford.

This is why Alyx is so incredible, Valve managed to make a modern FPS in to a VR game, despite the barriers that VR provides. They were then able to expand upon that and apply the immersive tech of VR to create a level of interaction within the game world that you very rarely see even from the most well-regarded VR games. Many developers are still finding their feet and learning to walk in VR - Valve hit the ground running with Alyx. There isn't a single other VR game I've played that provides the level of polish Alyx does. It's the definitive AAA experience that the medium seems to sorely need.

And while you'll hear people talk crap about it because it is VR exclusive, these people don't seem to understand that with the hype that's been building for 14 years regarding Half Life 3, there really was nothing else Valve could have done to live up to that hype: they needed something that pushed boundaries and blew minds and that's exactly what Alyx does - because of the immersion VR offers. It just wouldn't work as a flatscreen FPS, and if they did cave in and make it flatscreen it would probably get crapped on because it's 'just another shooter' like the community did with BattleZone - another game that is an amazing VR experience, but just 'meh' on a monitor.

If you have a VR headset, this is the killer app. All we can hope for now is that other developers will look at it and say 'Holy shit, we can do that!' and help push the medium even further.

Half-Life Alyx – A Love Letter to Gravity, Headcrabs and Classic PC Gamers

I have been playing Half Life since the days of smoky internet cafés, Gauss jumps on Crossfire and 60 Hz CRT monitors buzzing on the desk. So when I say Half Life Alyx did not just meet my expectations but stepped over them and looked back as if asking “You still with me?”, that should tell you something.

This is not just a good VR game. This is a real Half Life game that exists inside VR and it respects both identities.

A World That Feels Built Around Your Hands

City 17 in Alyx does not only look good, it feels physically present. You do not admire the world from a distance. You poke it, search through it and move things around simply because you wonder if you can. And the game constantly answers yes.

Drawers open the way someone actually looking for ammo would open them. You draw on dirty windows, flip bottles with your wrist and stack random junk out of curiosity. Nothing feels like a tech demo. Everything aims to immerse you. The detail is so strong that you find yourself behaving like a real person in a real place, not like someone sprinting between objective markers.

Story: Familiar DNA With a New Angle

I went in with concerns. A prequel starring Alyx in a timeline we roughly know. Could it really surprise me?

It does.

The writing is tight, efficient and quietly emotional. Alyx is not Gordon with dialogue. She is her own character, sarcastic, resilient and human in a way that fits perfectly into the Half Life universe. Her conversations with Russell balance tension and humor without weakening the atmosphere.

And since this is Valve, the ending does not simply work. It reshapes how you view the entire series. If Half Life has lived in your mind for decades, Alyx touches very old nerves in very new ways.

Gunplay: Slow, Precise and Stressful in the Best Way

If you come from chaotic and fast old school shooters like I do, Alyx feels like time has been slowed just enough to make every movement count.

There is no lazy hip fire. You line up your shots, steady your hand, peek from behind cover and physically duck as bullets snap past your head. Reloading becomes a small moment of panic: eject the magazine, grab a new one, slam it in and rack the slide, all while a headcrab zombie screams at you from a few feet away.

The weapon selection is small but intentional. Every gun feels unique. Upgrades change how the weapon behaves, not just the numbers. A reflex sight or a shotgun grenade launcher changes your entire approach to combat.

VR Design Done the Right Way

Alyx shows what happens when a studio designs for VR from the start instead of adapting a flat game.

Movement options are thoughtful and accessible. The gravity gloves are a brilliant piece of design. You point at an item, flick your wrist and catch it in the air. It feels like grounded science fiction and quickly becomes second nature.

Interactions are consistent. If something looks like you can grab it, you can. Doors behave like real doors. Ladders behave like real ladders. Your brain stops asking “Will this work?” and simply continues the experience.

Most VR games eventually show cracks in the illusion. In Alyx, those cracks are rare.

Atmosphere and Horror: Effective Without Cheap Tricks

The game understands that VR horror is different. A headcrab jumping at your face while your flashlight shakes in your hand is not the same as seeing it on a screen.

Alyx uses this smartly. It relies on sound, darkness and tension instead of sudden jump scares. Jeff deserves a mention without spoilers, because it is a sequence you remember as an experience, not just a level.

Audio, Music and Overall Polish

The sound design is outstanding. The creak of metal, the hiss of Combine radios and the wet growls of enemies that get too close all reinforce the world around you.

The soundtrack is subtle and reserved. It steps in only when necessary and always at the right moment.

The polish is clear everywhere: animations, lighting, physics and environmental storytelling all feel deliberate and refined.

Performance and Comfort

Technically, Alyx feels like a VR game where the engine and art team work in complete harmony. Once you tune your settings, performance stays stable.

Comfort options are flexible. New players can ease into it while experienced VR users can play with full freedom.

This is a game that respects your senses just as much as your hardware.

Verdict: The New Benchmark

Half Life Alyx is not perfect, but it is the closest VR has come to a complete and uncompromising AAA single player experience that truly understands the platform.

As someone who grew up with Half Life and spent decades trying to recapture that feeling, I can say without hesitation that Alyx is not only nostalgia. It is a preview of the future of immersive storytelling.

If you have a VR headset and still have not played it, you are not saving it for later. You are delaying one of the best experiences VR has to offer.

I remember partway through my first playthrough, I was hit by a wave of sadness, as I realised I must not have very much game left to experience, and the sombre knowledge that I'd never play another VR game that could possibly stand a chance of measuring up to it.

That feeling passed, as it turns out I was only a quarter of the way through at that point in time, but the latter sentiment has held true. Nothing could compare.

Half-Life Alyx is far from a vertical slice or a tech demo; it's a full fledged AAA experience that reminds you of when AAA meant something more than "a big company made it". Further than that, it's built to take full advantage of everything VR has to offer, and spares no expense giving you the experience in the most polished format imaginable.

I said it then and I'll say it now, HL:A is the best game I've ever played. I don't say this lightly. Devil May Cry 3 and 5 hold special places in my heart, as do the Halo and Ace Attorney trilogies, and friends of mine know how badly I'll shill Marvel vs Capcom 3 and Burnout Paradise. Doom, Steins;Gate, Monster Hunter, Left 4 Dead, there's an ocean of amazing games out there that belong in the category of peak, and among them, stands Half-Life Alyx, towering over them.

An experience you truly cannot get anywhere else, and one that I highly doubt can ever be replicated. A game that playing with a mouse & keyboard would be doing an immense disservice to yourself. I cannot in good conscience recommend VR as a platform, but should you ever find yourself wanting, or have an opportunity with a weekend at a friend's house, please. Do yourself a favour. Play this game.

I don't get the negative reviews on this game. 

"The combats too boring! Every enemy is just a bullet sponge!"
It was designed for dramatic, theatrical gameplay, not for boss fights that take multiple deaths to beat. If you look at the game at a pure difficulty stand point, then it's basically just a walking simulator with occasional puzzles, and I think thats fine. I wouldn't want to spend my time stuck on an extremely difficult boss fight, especially not in vr, where you will get exhausted and frustrated much faster.

"Theres too little weapon variety! Why is only one-handed guns?"
If they chose to add another gun, what would it be? A sniper rifle in a game thats mostly small rooms? An automatic rifle when theres already the pistol and smg? They already have every base covered with the pistol, shotgun, and smg, they even have a grenade launcher upgrade. Two handed weapons also didn't fit with how the game was geared towards newer vr players who likely don't have gunstocks. A lot of combat is also ducking in and out of cover, something that two handed guns make frustrating because they would constantly get caught.

Most other negative reviews are also just refuted instantly by developer commentary. 

"Why are there no melee weapons?"
Because of the lack of physical feedback, melee combat was just a huge immersion breaker for playtesters. They were basically just wiggling their controller infront of them, swinging at ghosts. I also feel like melee combat would've been bad for the game because they would either need to lower the ammo given, or make melee combat useless past the early game.

"Puzzles are too easy!"
Every puzzle was designed with the knowledge you already have, its not going to suddenly throw a new mechanic into your face and tell you to just figure it out. None of the puzzles felt incoherent or nonsensical, they always had logical solutions that feel rewarding to figure out. If you thought the puzzles were "too easy" then I guess your just some gaming guru that just hates figuring out sensible puzzles.

To get this out of the way: No, this game NEEDS to be VR to work, it just has to be. There are many mechanics and other things in this game that would not work on a simple mouse and keyboard. The gunplay is solid, even if you don't get as many guns as you do in Half-Life 2 or 1 and the Gravity Gloves? Fucking amazing. I do have to admit though, the upgrade system is uh... meh. It's kinda just... there? Graphics are fucking solid and it sure feels good to see an FPS on Source 2 now, after kinda not seeing anything like it for so long apart from Dota 2 (no differences lol) and some small VR games that have a cartoony artstyle anyway. The LOD are also weird at times, but again, it's not that bad. 
There is plenty of cool details on stuff too, like when you throw a full glass bottle of something on the floor, you get a little puddle of water or whatever on the ground. Lots of signs are readable finally and have funny things in there sometimes. It's overall just amazing.

Sounds are solid and really good. Plenty of cool ambience noises, details and more. The harder you hit your gun on something for example, it makes a completely different noise. Ambience and variour other things set in the mood, guns sound great, the Combines sound great too (though nothing will top the original one from HL2.) are great, Headcrabs and other monsters we know from HL2 sound scary and incredible.

The music is... uhhh... good. But nothing too fancy to say about it, really. It's not HL2 music and nothing will come close to it, but it still sounds pretty good and does a good job. Bit bummed out I couldn't hear the Trailer music anyway though.

Story? Well, I am not gonna say much, but ooooooooooooooh boy... the story is good. That's all. Seriously, it's good.

Overall... this game is a masterpiece. It's a Half-Life game from start to finish, it's perfect and I love it. And most importantly:

10/10 (mild spoilers ahead)

What I have noticed so far from VR is that the platform is still going through rough development. Titles are either very disappointing, rely on a single gimmick or not optimized. 

The gimmick ones are simple: Wall runs, pilot sims or shooters. They have one thing and one thing only that works, so they base their entire game off of it. The non optimized ones you can find all through steam, just take a look at Fallout. If the modding community did not exist, the vr experience wouldn't even be properly playable. Finally the disappointments: smaller indie titles that lure you in with promises, but don't deliver. Perhaps even more developed games that just did not get the attention to detail that the VR space needs. 

Enter Half Life: Alyx, a game that does not just have shooting, movement and a good story... but also great combat, immersive/trippy experiences, beautiful visuals, diversity in gameplay and the most fun yet basic puzzles I have ever had the pleasure of experiencing. What this game does right is that it takes all the elements of a proper video game and translates it into the right VR experience. No other VR game is able to actually have a proper story with fitting gameplay and polished mechanics. 

If this entire game would be a desktop experience it would be the most OK game ever made. However, the reason it deserves a 10/10 is because the game is able to implement and merge VR into it's core design. 

A very good examples are the puzzles. Super straight forward VR puzzles that are just that much more distinguishable BECAUSE you are in VR. Puzzles that are wayy too simple for a desktop experience yet so immersive in a VR one. These should serve as the guideline for all future VR puzzle games to come. 

The gravity gloves are the most simple yet immersive way of implementing the: "flick" mechanic. Most games just included it in some way or another to grab objects easier. Here it has an in-universe experience and serves one of your main tools throughout the game. It is incredibly fun to throw barrels around, toss items at the ceiling tongues or grab a last-minute heal off of an enemy to survive. Nothing here is mind breaking- Just very well implemented. 

Now the weapons and combat. I am more than happy to announce that this game only has 3 weapons. 4 fetched out well serving weapons all having their positives and negatives. All of them have unique ammo that you can salvage around the area's or tucked away in hidden boxes. You never really run out of ammo even if you miss a fair amount of shots. You always feel the need to preserve ammo yet you cannot be too trigger happy. The upgrades and attachments are all sweet and simple. Enemy variety is spot on as each enemy has an optimal way to be dealt with. There is no need for the game to go overboard in upgrades or combat. It's straight forward and fits very well with the exploration.
Small shout out to Jeff. It was more than genius what the developers did with him and how fluent the experience was. By far my most favourite moment of the whole game! 

Next up is the games pacing. The game accelerates about as clean as possible. The beginning only containing easy to deal with enemies so you can get used to the VR combat and atmosphere. Once you get the shotgun the game stats to ramp up a bit. My favourite here was the introduction of the grenades. A very simple thing, yet so satisfying when done well. Not to mention each introduction has a small section of the game dedicated to it. For example, when you first encounter the mines it is set as an example so you can get used to them. Textbook game design, yet, something that is missing other titles. 

Now the overall progression and visual design. I absolutely love the amount of information this game withholds. Only when you need to jump or climb does the game hint you how to make it work. Everything else is up to you. Don't know where to go? How about you look around and find a creative solution. There is nothing that points you towards the right direction except your own logic and patience. I was delighted to find out I had to throw a grenade though a vent to enter to the next area. It took me 45 minutes and a locker filled with explosives to figure it out, but I had fun trying to find a solution the entire time. 
Throughout the entire game I definitely had to take a small break and look around. The city streets and design of the alien lifeforms was beautiful to look at. It most definitely feels like you are inside of the old half life universe, they nailed that part.

Finally the negatives. While I cannot find anything bad to say about the gameplay, visuals or story itself, I have had problems with the performance. I ran this game on the Quest 2 linked to my pc. Overall it was fine, however there were moments were the game lagged down to a stunning 10 fps until I rebooted the headset. Another big issue was the game crashing during any loading screen bugging out the pc-link connection that I had. Every time this happened my Quest was not able to find my PC anymore so I had to reboot both devices in order to link them again. Simply killing the application in task manager and re-opening it did not help. This was a smaller problem as it only happened around ~5 times and it could most definitely be a problem on my end. As the game barely stuttered or lagged during the gameplay I won't hold it 100% accountable. 

In conclusion: This is by far the best VR game I have played due to it's polish and execution. It has many different VR elements thrown into a single package. It's not just combat, puzzles or story. It's all of them combined for a fun and intriguing experience.

Arguably, the best VR game released so far, and definitely the one I've had the most fun playing. But it's not only great "for a vr game" it's also a great game, period, and an excellent entry to the Half-Life series.

The Gravity Gloves take some getting used to at first, especially to select the correct target, but eventually become so second-nature that you might find yourself trying to use them in real life after a long session.

Combat feels good overall, although in the harder difficulties, the enemies feel like bullet sponges at times. But even then, you usually have multiple ways to dispose of them, using the environment or even other enemies, and finding cover behind obstacles feels particularly immersive in VR. A few more weapons variety would have been great, but I understand the decision to trim the usual half-life arsenal into a few more fleshed out weapons with their own upgrade system for simplicity's sake.

Exploration is where Alyx shines the brightest, from scavenging the area for resources, to searching how to open the way forward. You will find appealign environments and set pieces, It feels rewarding and interesting throughout the game. However, the repeatable puzzles, like the infamous orb puzzles are not that great, and they overstay their welcome, but they are a relatively minor issue in the face of everything else that the game offers.

Visually, Alyx reaches a stunning level for a VR game, and it holds up great even in spectating mode. I feel like I need to make an aside for the character animations and especially for whoever is responsible for the first vortigaunt encounter, it is in a league of its own.

But, my favourite moment in Alyx is That one. If you have played, you know which one I'm talking about, and I don't think it would be possible to replicate that secuence effectively in any other medium apart from VR. but I won't spoil it for you, you'll have to find out the rest on your own.

[h1]NoVR mod experience[/h1]
Okay so
The game has 98% positive reviews
With that said - this game is probably the only valid reason for you to buy the VR set
Unless you dont have enough budget/big enough room/problems with wearing such a thing

But since NoVR mod (on ModDB) is working pretty great and will have neat updates in the future, we gotta look into that deeper.

[h1]Main features[/h1]
Visuals, immersion and the huge level of details in level design - if you like this stuff - you will love this game. With or without VR - this game takes you in and you will struggle to leave.
Liquid physics, lighting, props everywhere, great optimization on an average PC. There a lot to tell.
Basically, its a very neat tech demo for Source 2.

[h1]But you are not Gordon Freeman and you do not have the HEV suit[/h1]
Now, if you came here for amazing gun blazing gameplay - dont expect a lot. You will shoot stuff from time to time, solve some basic puzzles(some are not present in Non-VR atm), some of which will require a standart awareness of your surroundings. Frankly, Half-Life 2 wasn't that great with shooting either, but in this game, if you play Below Hard - you will be bored, probably. On hard though - enemies are just bullet sponges. Although its cool that almost every enemy has a little trick to beat him fast like - shoot a propane tank, a parasite, or throw a grenade, or wait for him to reload etc, etc. There's really not too much enemies or their variety so yeah, there's that.

Also, there's lots of looting, scavenging and an okay-ish upgrade system (some of which are not present in Non-VR atm)

[h1]Embrace "Combined" Earth[/h1]
The events of the game - is a prequel to HL2 with an amazing twist at the end, though, expectable.
You are Alyx Vance - a rebel who will be dragged in some dramatic events pretty soon after start of the game. 
You will meet a couple of new characters, destroy a lot of property, explore some weird places and shoot a bunch of angry soldiers. At the end - well, there's a lot.
Expect lots of easter eggs and nostalgia emotions.
Soundtrack is...eh, its forgettable, in comparison to HL2+Episodes music. While the sound design is pretty great.
Level design is awesome, lots of things to mess around with (like the famous piano, pool table, touching everything you see)
Dialogues between Alyx and Russel (her partner-in-crime so to speak) are pretty cute and occasionally funny
And as for replay factor - only if you wanna hang around the whole game with the Damn Gnome. Or wanna play Fan Addons.

This is a bloody masterpiece. First proper AAA+ VR title, and will be remembered as the ushering in the age of VR gaming, just as Valve ushered in the new era of PC gaming with Steam (along with HL2) back in the day.

Tutorialization and easing in of the player: 
Perfectly balanced, eases the player into every element step by step. It does not throw you into ridiculous shooting matches at the beginning. Pacing is therefore brilliant.

Graphics: These are the best graphics I have ever seen in VR.

Performance: I have a very demanding Pimax 8KX (4K native per eye, 150-170 FOV @ 90 hz), and a 3080 Ti. Some lesser games perform much worse than HL Alyx. This game has a very clever and effective auto-tuning of graphics settings, so that you always maintain playable framerates.

Gameplay mechanics: They have taken some of the best ideas of VR design that have already been established by others (and by Valve), and put all the best pieces into this. The use of the index controllers is done masterfully, though it can be tricky to get used to some things, like don't put the right thumb on the thumb touchpad when you want to pick up things, as you will inadvertently get the quick-select menu (weapon, hand or multitool).

Audio: Fantastic.
